articles.title: Sweden to ban forever chemicals from kitchens and clothing by 2028
articles.summary:
BY THE OPTIMIST DAILY EDITORIAL TEAM Sweden announced on July 23 that it will ban per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances from consumer products by January 1, 2028. The list covers clothing, shoes, waterproofing agents, kitchenware, cosmetics, and ski wax. “This is a major victory for human health and for the Swedish environment,” said Minister for Climate […]
The post Sweden to ban forever chemicals from kitchens and clothing by 2028 first appeared on The Optimist Daily: Making Solutions the News.
articles.content:
BY THE OPTIMIST DAILY EDITORIAL TEAM

Sweden announced on July 23 that it will ban per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances from consumer products by January 1, 2028. The list covers clothing, shoes, waterproofing agents, kitchenware, cosmetics, and ski wax. “This is a major victory for human health and for the Swedish environment,” said Minister for Climate and the Environment Romina Pourmokhtari.

France moved first, banning PFAS products in 2026 wherever safer alternatives exist. Denmark banned them on food contact paper and board in 2020, then extended that to clothing, footwear, and waterproofing agents in 2026. Sweden is the third EU member state to act. The European Commission has not yet put forward its own proposal.

What Sweden’s ban will cover in 2028

The restrictions apply only where PFAS-free alternatives are already available, which takes one of the industry’s standard objections off the table: that switching away from these chemicals isn’t yet technically feasible. Products covered include clothing, shoes, waterproofing agents, kitchenware, cosmetics, and ski wax.

“Sweden does not intend to wait while forever chemicals continue to spread in our homes, in nature and in our bodies,” Pourmokhtari said.

“Sweden’s proposal proves that governments don’t have to accept toxic chemistry as the price of modern life,” said Sian Sutherland, co-founder of A Plastic Planet. “Safer alternatives already exist, and Sweden has shown that governments can and should choose to back them.”

Why PFAS became impossible to keep ignoring

PFAS are a group of more than 10,000 synthetic chemicals used since the 1940s, found in products from nonstick cookware to firefighting foam. They degrade over thousands of years. They have turned up at the summit of Mount Everest and in human blood samples from every region of the world.

That’s the contamination picture. The health evidence is what has been forcing action. Chronic PFAS exposure has been linked to certain cancers, reduced fertility, and immune system disruption, with the greatest documented risk falling on pregnant women and children in the first 1,000 days of life, when effects can persist into the next generation.

“PFAS don’t stay locked inside products. They escape into our homes, our food and water and our bodies,” said Sutherland.

Where the EU stands on PFAS restrictions

The European Commission is expected to present legislative proposals in 2027. A scientific opinion published in March recommended broad restrictions on forever chemicals in consumer products. The European Chemicals Agency is due to add a second opinion on the socio-economic impact of those measures before the end of this year.

After a proposal is put forward, full EU-wide implementation takes several more years. The expected regulations would restrict PFAS in consumer products including clothing and food packaging, with exceptions carved out for medical devices and other strategic sectors.

EU-wide drinking water protections against PFAS took effect in January 2026, though they drew criticism for addressing contamination at the tap rather than stopping it upstream. Roughly 12.5 million people in Europe currently live in communities with PFAS-contaminated drinking water.

“The solutions are here. What has been missing is the political will,” Sutherland said. France, Denmark, and Sweden have stopped waiting for Brussels to reach the same conclusion.

articles.title: Rare piglet the size of 'a grapefruit with legs' born at zoo
articles.summary: Rana's arrival is described as a "lifeline for the species", which is in rapid decline in the wild.
articles.content:
An endangered piglet the size of a "grapefruit with legs" when she was born has made her debut at Chester Zoo, conservationists have said.

Rana - a babirusa known as a "pig-deer" - has been described as a "lifeline for the species" which is in rapid decline in the wild.

Babirusas in the wild are found on just four Indonesian islands and the zoo said they were being wiped out due to African swine fever reaching the islands five years ago.

The attraction's Hannah Owens said Rana was "tiny" when she was born but has "grown a lot and is doing really well".

Until recently, babirusas were considered vulnerable to extinction by the International Union for the Conservation of Nature, external, but are due to be upgraded to "critically endangered", the zoo said.

Rana is the fifth piglet born to mother Matano, who was herself born at Chester Zoo 11 years ago and now has descendants living in zoos across Europe.

Owens said while babirusas "are doing well in our care" numbers in the wild were "radically reducing" and it would be "horrendous if they disappeared, because they were amazing, charismatic animals".

She added: "Piglets like Rana are a lifeline for the species."

Unlike most pigs, babirusas typically have just one or two offspring at a time rather than large litters - one reason their numbers recover slowly when wild populations are hit hard.

New mothers are also highly sensitive to disturbance, so keepers kept an eye on Rana and Matano remotely via a baby monitor until the pair were ready to be seen in public.
articles.reasoning: The birth of an endangered babirusa piglet at Chester Zoo represents a significant conservation success, providing hope for a species rapidly declining in the wild due to disease. The story highlights tangible efforts to preserve biodiversity with broad ecological importance and detailed context about the species' status and breeding challenges.

**What happened** – Chester Zoo recently welcomed a tiny babirusa piglet named Rana. When she was born, she was about the size of a grapefruit with legs. Rana is the fifth baby born to her mother, Matano, who was also born at Chester Zoo 11 years ago. Keepers carefully watched Rana and Matano with a baby monitor until they were ready to be seen by visitors.

**Impact** – Rana’s birth is important because babirusas usually have only one or two babies at a time, so their numbers grow slowly. Since wild babirusas are rapidly disappearing, every new baby born in zoos helps keep the species alive. Rana and her family are part of a breeding program that supports babirusas in zoos across Europe, providing a safety net for the species.

**What’s next step** – The zoo will continue to care for Rana and Matano while helping raise awareness about babirusas and their challenges. Conservationists hope that by protecting these animals in zoos and supporting their natural habitats, the babirusa’s decline in the wild can be slowed or even reversed.

**One-sentence takeaway** – The birth of Rana, a tiny endangered babirusa piglet, is a vital step in saving a species facing rapid extinction in the wild.

articles.title: A new type of levee is taking root in Northern California
articles.content:
Visitors to the Palo Alto Baylands Nature Preserve, captivated by gliding birds overhead and golden hills across the Bay waters, could be forgiven for failing to notice that the preserve is also home to the Bay’s newest levee.

Most levees look like steep, barren embankments or riprap-clad seawalls, designed to prevent flooding by adding extra feet of height. But this project, though it shares a name, is a different type of infrastructure altogether. Seeded with over 35 species of native plants, the site is a pilot for what’s known as a horizontal levee, or living levee, blending into the estuary’s natural scenery as it spreads its feet of added height over a longer area.

In stark contrast to a traditional levee, the Palo Alto Horizontal Levee Pilot Project’s natural appearance and gradual slope are designed to interact with Bay waters the same way natural estuaries do.

“When you look at levees that are along the bay front, a lot of times they’ve got really steep faces and big, huge rocks in front of them to protect them from wind waves,” explained Mark Lindley, lead engineer on the Palo Alto living levee. “By having this flat, gradual slope with really dense vegetation on it instead of having rock, the waves break on that slope like they do on a beach.”

To support our nonprofit environmental journalism, please consider disabling your ad-blocker to allow ads on Grist. Here's How

The project is part of a growing trend in California’s Bay Area of using this type of green infrastructure to provide both flood mitigation and habitat restoration. Completed in 2017, the Oro Loma Horizontal Levee near Hayward, California, was the first of its kind and informed the design of the Palo Alto project, and others. There are around a dozen in various stages of design and development around the Bay.

But the Palo Alto pilot project is the first to be hydrologically connected to the Bay. Beneath the plants, soil, and gravel layers, plumbing connects the slope of the horizontal levee to the Palo Alto Wastewater Treatment Center across the street, allowing treated wastewater to irrigate the levee’s plants. As it does, the plants remove nitrogen from the water before it then filters into the Bay. Nitrogen, which can lead to harmful algal blooms in excess, is generally high in wastewater — though, the water from the facility currently meets regulations to be released into the Bay, said Samantha Engelage, senior engineer for the City of Palo Alto. The added treatment is purely a bonus for water quality.

A sign explains the horizontal levee pilot project to visitors at the Baylands Nature Preserve. Visitors are also encouraged to submit photos to help researchers monitor the site. Charlotte Burks

By mimicking the natural world, the horizontal levee also provides the conditions native species need to thrive. One beloved Bay Area resident that may benefit from the approach is the salt-marsh harvest mouse, affectionately known as “salties.” The cinnamon-colored rodents, which fit in the palm of a hand, climb vegetation to escape rising tides each day. But due to encroaching development, they’ve been listed as endangered for decades — and their niche habitat also makes them vulnerable to the changing climate. “All you need is a couple of really, really bad storm and tide events to knock out a [local] population,” said Katie Smith, a wildlife biologist and saltie expert.

By design, the horizontal levee will restore the vegetation and habitat that salties and other estuary wildlife rely on. According to Smith, the plan for the levee appears to create the “optimal potential option for salt-marsh harvest mice.”

To support our nonprofit environmental journalism, please consider disabling your ad-blocker to allow ads on Grist. Here's How

Stretching just 500 feet along the shore, the pilot project restores only a small portion of salties’ habitat — and it does not provide the full flood control needed at the Baylands. But it will provide something else: data. Over the next five years, researchers from the United States Geological Survey, universities, and local nonprofits will monitor qualitative benefits, such as recreational use, and quantitative benefits, like impacts on biodiversity and water quality. The results could help justify the higher costs often associated with green infrastructure projects like the horizontal levee, explained Engelage.

The project has been almost a decade in the making. And although the levee is now visible to observant visitors at Baylands Nature Preserve, it is not fully operational yet. According to Engelage, delays in the project have sprouted from complexities in connecting the plumbing from the wastewater treatment plant to the levee.

But its gentle slope is already acting as a flood break. And it is clear that for Bay Area residents big and small, the additional protection of this levee and others like it could not come too soon. In the Bay Area alone, sea level is projected to rise 3 to 6 feet by 2100. More imminently, the forecasted El Niño weather system could bring the Bay 6 inches of temporary sea level rise — a taste of what future decades may hold.

“Twenty years from now, what we see at king tides is just going to be a normal high tide,” said Lindley, referring to the highest tides of the year. “Those areas that we’re seeing flooded at king tide, they’ll be flooded every day.”

Correction: An earlier version of this story misstated Samantha Engelage’s title.
articles.reasoning: The article describes an innovative environmental infrastructure project—a horizontal living levee in Northern California—that combines flood protection with habitat restoration and water quality improvement. It has broad significance for climate resilience and biodiversity in the Bay Area, providing measurable benefits such as nitrogen removal from wastewater, habitat for endangered species, and flood mitigation. The project is well-detailed and represents a meaningful advancement in green infrastructure with potential for wider application.

articles.title: Guest Idea: Green Bins Are Spreading Faster Than the Habit of Using Them
articles.summary:

The post Guest Idea: Green Bins Are Spreading Faster Than the Habit of Using Them appeared first on Earth911.
articles.content:
Editor’s Note: This is a sponsored posting.

Curbside food scrap collection has spread fast. BioCycle’s nationwide survey counted 14.9 million U.S. households with access to food waste collection in 2023, up 49 percent from 10 million two years earlier.

Getting those bins used is the harder part. Reported participation runs from near-universal in a handful of cities to under 30 percent in others. That gap matters. Food waste is about 24 percent of what U.S. municipal landfills take in, and the EPA estimates it accounts for 58 percent of the fugitive methane those landfills release. An unused green bin isn’t a neutral outcome.

Quick definition first, since the name varies. The green bin is the curbside cart for household organics: food scraps, plus yard trimmings and food-soiled paper depending on your program. It’s collected separately from trash and recycling and sent to a composting or anaerobic digestion facility instead of a landfill. It isn’t green everywhere. Toronto runs a Green Bin program, New York City uses brown ones, and elsewhere it’s the organics cart, the compost cart, or the food scraps cart. What matters is where the material ends up, not the color.

Why People Quit the Green Bin

Households opt out for a long list of reasons: confusion about what’s accepted, forgetting collection day, plain inconvenience. I’d add one that gets less attention because it’s unglamorous. The bin gets disgusting, cleaning it turns into a recurring chore, and eventually the chore wins.

I’ll be straight that this is a hypothesis, not a documented finding. I haven’t found a study that isolates bin cleaning as a reason people quit. What I’ve got is the pattern I hear from customers constantly. But there’s evidence that making the job less unpleasant moves the numbers.

In 2023–24, Essex County Council in the UK ran a year-long Food Recycling Project. It delivered a package to more than 375,000 households: a sticker for the general waste bin, an information leaflet, and a free roll of compostable liners. Food recycling tonnage rose an average of 21 percent against a control group in the first three months after delivery, more than double the council’s 10 percent target.

The liners were one piece of that package, running alongside a media campaign, so the case study can’t tell us how much of the gain they drove on their own. What it does show is that handing people a tool to keep the mess contained belongs in the mix alongside better signage. It also shows the limit. Free liner giveaways are a subsidy most households will never get.

So the question isn’t whether a cleaner, contained bin helps people stick with the program. Plainly it does. The question is how you get there when nobody’s handing out free bags. That’s the gap BagEZ fills.

Doing More With Less

BagEZ holds a standard bag open inside the green bin, 13 gallons (49 liters) and up. Food scraps go into the bag, not against the cart. Everything stays contained, and the bin stays clean and dry. That’s aimed straight at the reason people give up: the cleaning.

It’s a folding steel rack with clips that lock the bag to the frame. The handles grip the bin’s rim and hold the bag open and suspended. On collection day you pull off the clips, seal the bag, and lift out the frame before setting the bin at the curb.

The size is up to you, and the data says most kitchens don’t need much. The MITRE-Gallup survey, the largest U.S. household food-waste study to date, surveyed nearly 10,000 households and put the average household’s food waste at 6.2 cups a week, or about 8.8 cups once you count peels, cores, and bones. That’s a bit over half a gallon. Even a household running well above average isn’t close to filling a big curbside cart with food scraps. So size the bag to your kitchen, not your bin. A 13-gallon bag is plenty for most households, it costs less than lining a full cart, and a right-sized bag is also what makes the odor tricks below work. Size up if your program takes yard trimmings too, or if collection runs every other week.

One caveat before you change anything: check what your program accepts. Liner rules vary a lot across North America. Some programs take certified compostable bags only, some want paper or newspaper, some want food scraps loose in the cart. A bag your hauler doesn’t accept can get your cart skipped and the whole load flagged for contamination. Earth911’s recycling search is a good place to start: earth911.com/recycling-search

After collection, a wipe with vinegar and water handles anything that’s built up. On a bin that’s stayed dry, that’s a seasonal job, not a weekly one, and you never have to drag out the hose.

The Green Bin Yuck Factor

Ever notice the puddle in the bottom of your countertop organics caddy after you pull the bag? That’s mostly moisture coming out of the food itself. Produce is largely water, and as it breaks down that water gets released.

The same thing happens in the curbside bin, at a bigger scale. Bags of scraps keep releasing moisture as they sit, and when a bag rests against the bottom and sides of the bin, that liquid builds up into the sticky residue that smells and makes the bin dirty.

BagEZ works differently because the bag never touches the bin. The frame holds it up and lets air move all the way around: underneath, the sides, everywhere. Condensation on the outside of the bag has nowhere to pool. It evaporates instead of collecting at the bottom, and the walls stay dry.

A right-sized bag makes the odor tricks work better, too. A sprinkle of baking soda in the small contained space around the bag does more than the same sprinkle spread thin across a big empty floor. Less smell, fewer flies. Fewer flies, no maggots.

Some people use food-grade diatomaceous earth against fly larvae. DE works by drying insects out, and it stops working the moment it gets wet, so a dry bin is a precondition for it doing anything at all. Same story as the baking soda: it only earns its keep in a dry, contained gap.

Two more that help, cheap. A few sheets of newspaper under the bag catch drips if a bag ever fails. And a cloth sachet of peppermint and cloves tied to the outside of the bin throws off raccoons and rodents, which hunt almost entirely by smell. A bin that doesn’t smell like food stops being worth their trouble.

Why It Works

The infrastructure is already there. The bins are at the curb, the trucks run, and the environmental case, going by the numbers up top, isn’t in question. What’s been missing is a cheap, fast way to keep the bin clean enough that people don’t quietly give up on it.

A reusable steel frame that holds a bag open sounds too simple to matter. That’s sort of the point. The bin stays clean, the habit stays easy, and food scraps end up where they’re meant to.

Set it next to the alternatives and the difference is in how each one works. Bin cleaning services deal with the problem after it happens, on a schedule, for a recurring fee. Full-size liners cost money every week and are sized to the bin, not to what you actually throw out. A frame is a one-time buy that works with the bag size your household already uses.

A green bin program only works if people keep using it, and people keep using what doesn’t gross them out. That’s the hinge the whole thing turns on. Take away the wet mess on the walls and most of the reasons to quit go with it: nothing pooling at the bottom, nothing to hose out, no smell pulling animals across the yard. The bin stays clean on its own, week after week, with a bag you were going to buy anyway.

Size it to your kitchen instead of your bin, clip it to the frame, and the green bin stops being the chore you avoid. Find it at bagez.com.

articles.personality_title_es: Nueva herramienta ayuda a mantener limpios los botes verdes y fomenta el reciclaje de residuos alimentarios
articles.personality_presentation_es:
**Contexto**
Muchas ciudades en Estados Unidos han comenzado programas donde las personas pueden poner restos de comida y desechos de jardín en botes especiales llamados botes verdes. Estos botes se recogen por separado y su contenido se convierte en compost en lugar de ir a los vertederos. Esto ayuda a reducir gases dañinos como el metano que producen los vertederos.

**Qué pasó**
Aunque más hogares ahora tienen botes verdes, muchos no los usan regularmente porque se ensucian y huelen mal, lo que hace que limpiarlos sea una tarea desagradable. Una empresa canadiense llamada BagEZ creó un marco de acero reutilizable que sostiene una bolsa abierta dentro del bote. Esto mantiene los restos de comida contenidos y evita que se acumule humedad dentro del bote. El marco facilita sacar la bolsa y mantiene el bote limpio sin necesitar bolsas especiales ni lavados frecuentes.

**Impacto**
Esta solución simple aborda un gran problema que hace que la gente deje de usar los botes verdes. Al mantener los botes secos y sin olor, BagEZ anima a usar más seguido los programas de reciclaje de residuos alimentarios. Esto puede reducir la cantidad de desperdicios de comida en los vertederos, disminuyendo las emisiones de metano que contribuyen al cambio climático. También ahorra tiempo y esfuerzo a las personas que limpian sus botes.

**Próximo paso**
A medida que más personas conozcan herramientas como BagEZ, les será más fácil seguir usando los botes verdes. Los programas de residuos podrían promover estas soluciones para mejorar la participación. Los usuarios deben revisar las reglas locales sobre tipos de bolsas antes de usarlas. La empresa sigue ofreciendo este producto en línea para ayudar a más hogares a mantener hábitos sostenibles.

**Resumen en una frase**
Un simple marco de acero llamado BagEZ ayuda a mantener los botes verdes limpios y secos, facilitando y haciendo más popular el reciclaje de residuos alimentarios.
